lesson.title: Bargaining Over the Postwar World at Yalta
lesson.summary: In February 1945, with victory in Europe approaching after D-Day and the atomic bomb still a closely guarded secret, the leaders of the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union met at Yalta to shape the postwar world, decisions that later drew heavy criticism as the Cold War began.
lesson.body:
By February 1945, the direction of the war had become clear. Allied forces that had landed at Normandy the previous June were pushing into Germany from the west, while Soviet forces advanced from the east, and Germany's defeat appeared to be only a matter of time. With victory approaching in Europe, but the war against Japan still expected to require a costly campaign, the leaders of the three major Allied powers, often called the Big Three, met to plan for the world that would follow the fighting.

From February 4 to 11, 1945, President Franklin Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin gathered at Yalta, a resort town in Crimea, then part of the Soviet Union. The three leaders reached agreements on several major questions. Germany, once defeated, would be divided into occupation zones controlled separately by the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union. The conference also produced a Declaration on Liberated Europe, in which the Allied powers pledged to help liberated nations hold free elections and establish democratic governments, a promise the Soviet Union would not keep in the Eastern European countries its army occupied. The leaders also began laying groundwork for a new international body meant to prevent future wars, which became the United Nations.

Because the atomic bomb had not yet been tested and the invasion of Japan was still expected to be extremely difficult, American planners at Yalta placed real value on securing Soviet help against Japan. Stalin agreed that the Soviet Union would enter the war against Japan within roughly three months after Germany's surrender, in exchange for territorial concessions in East Asia. The Soviet Union kept this commitment, declaring war on Japan in early August 1945, in the same week the atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

Yalta later became one of the most criticized diplomatic meetings in American history. Critics argued that Roosevelt, who was seriously ill and would die just two months later in April 1945, conceded too much influence over Eastern Europe to Stalin, effectively allowing Soviet domination of the region to take hold despite the promises about free elections. As Soviet control over Eastern Europe hardened into what would soon be called the Iron Curtain, Yalta came to be remembered less as a moment of Allied unity and more as an early, uneasy preview of the Cold War rivalry that would define the following decades.
